sections.title: People & Politics
sections.description: Important developments in governments, societies and the people shaping the world.

cards.title: Woman killed in West Bank violence, Israeli army investigates
cards.content: A 72-year-old Palestinian woman, Fadda al-Fahidat, was shot and killed outside her home in the West Bank village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho. According to Palestinian accounts, the violence started with settler harassment, followed by the woman's son, Arafat, trying to help the injured and being shot himself. Israeli authorities claim that Palestinians carried out a car-ramming attack and then threw rocks, prompting the settlers to open fire. The Israeli army says Fadda was killed by a civilian settler, while the Palestinian health ministry reports multiple wounded. The Israeli military and police have launched an investigation. High tensions have been reported in the area since a group of settlers moved into eight houses on November 4, with some residents and activists describing a campaign of settler attacks and intimidation.

cards.title: Pakistan's national grid struggles to compete with solar boom
cards.content: In Pakistan, the use of solar panels has increased significantly since 2018, with seven million households now owning panels. The shift is driven by individual households seeking to escape soaring electricity prices from the unreliable national grid, which has more than doubled in a few years. While the solar boom brings benefits, concerns also arise about the national grid's financial burden, as people abandon the grid, leading to increased costs and a potential 'utility death spiral'. The government aims to make the grid more competitive to offer better energy prices, renegotiating contracts and focusing on efficiency, as Pakistan's energy minister warns of the need to avoid this trend.

sections.title: Science and technology
sections.description: Discover breakthroughs in science, space, computing and emerging technology.

cards.title: Scientists capture molecular images of bacteria ends in breakthrough
cards.content: Scientists at University College London have made a groundbreaking discovery, capturing the first-ever molecular-resolution images of the ends of rod-shaped bacteria. This breakthrough has revealed previously unseen structural features, which could help researchers understand why some bacteria respond differently to antibiotics. To achieve this, the researchers developed a unique method to immobilize the bacteria on a specially treated glass surface, allowing them to examine their exposed tips, or poles, at the molecular level. The images showed that the bacterial poles change with cellular activity, with rapidly dividing bacteria displaying fold-like defects, while less active cells had smoother poles. The study also found structural differences between species, which could influence how they interact with antibiotics. The researchers believe that their discovery could lead to the development of new treatments for drug-resistant bacteria.

cards.title: Gulf of Mexico deep-sea species face extinction risk due to genetic changes
cards.content: A new study led by researchers at Florida International University finds that some deep-sea species in the Gulf of Mexico may be vulnerable to extinction due to changes in their genetic makeup. The study examined genetic data from five species of fish and shrimp and found that all of them showed genetic warning signs associated with increased extinction risk. One species of lanternfish had lost around 8% of its genetic diversity over just 12 years, which is comparable to losses recorded in some threatened and endangered animals over longer periods. The findings suggest that some deep-sea populations may have already been genetically vulnerable before the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill, making them more susceptible to environmental disturbances. The study highlights the importance of considering genetic diversity and long-term viability when assessing the health of marine ecosystems, and suggests that traditional population counts may not reveal the full extent of the threats facing deep-sea species.

cards.title: Spain Proposes Stricter Rules for Data Centers to Boost Renewable Energy
cards.content: Spain's government is pushing to impose stricter rules on data centers, a booming industry in the country. The proposal, which doesn't require parliamentary approval, aims to ensure that 80% of electricity used by data centers comes from renewable sources. This measure has sparked concerns among investors, including Amazon, Microsoft, and Blackstone-backed QTS, as it could cost the industry billions of dollars in investment. The move is widely expected to pass ahead of the November 29 elections and is seen as a key issue in the political debate. Aragón, a region in the country's northeast, is at the center of the opposition to the draft rules, with concerns over the impact on the region's natural resources, noise, and water use.

sections.title: Health & wellness
sections.description: Medical research, public health and discoveries that affect everyday wellbeing.

cards.title: GlioTrace Reveals Brain Cancer Cell Behavior Insights
cards.content: Researchers at Uppsala University have developed a new method called GlioTrace that allows them to watch thousands of glioblastoma cells move through living brain tissue, revealing how they change their behavior over time. This aggressive brain cancer is difficult to contain because its cells can spread deep into surrounding healthy tissue. GlioTrace uses automated microscopy and machine learning to follow individual cancer cells as they travel through brain tissue, showing that cells do not all spread in the same way. The method also revealed that glioblastoma cells are remarkably adaptable, changing their shape and movement patterns over just a few days. The findings could help researchers better understand why this cancer is so difficult to contain and develop treatments that stop tumor cells from spreading.

cards.title: UK Extends Palantir Contract to 2029 to Manage Hospital Waiting Lists
cards.content: The UK government has decided to extend its contract with US technology giant Palantir, worth £330m, until 2029 to manage hospital waiting lists in England. The initial contract was due to end in 2031, but the government will now invite British firms to bid for the contract from 2029. Palantir, which has been criticized for its involvement in Israel's use of technology in the Gaza conflict and US immigration enforcement, has been involved in the project since 2024. The government's decision has sparked concerns about the use of patient data, with some politicians calling for a change to avoid overdependence on one supplier. Palantir has defended its work, saying it is exceeding targets and helping to deliver more operations and reduce waiting times.

sections.title: Environment
sections.description: Climate, oceans, ecosystems and the changing planet around us.

cards.title: CO2 Emissions Reach 40 Billion Tonnes, Threatening 1.5°C Threshold
cards.content: The world's CO2 emissions have increased to nearly 40 billion tonnes per year due to fossil-fuel-driven industrialisation, causing the planet to warm by about 1.3-1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. If everyone lived like the average American, the warming would be around 3.7°C, while living like the average Qatari would push warming to over 5°C. On the other hand, if everyone lived like the average Indian, the warming would be lower, at around 0.8°C. Historically, the Chinese lifestyle has had a much lower impact, with warming of only 1.2°C. The United Nations Environment Programme warns that overshooting the 1.5°C threshold is likely within the next three to four years.

cards.title: Human metabolism's carbon dioxide emissions rise 74% in 30 years
cards.content: A new study by the University of Bath has found that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased by 74% over the past three decades, with the global total reaching an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons annually by 2015. The study, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO2 production in people of all ages and found that the increase is mainly due to population growth, with more than 60% of the rise attributed to an increase in the number of people rather than a significant change in the amount produced by each individual. The researchers suggest that accounting for this activity could help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.

cards.title: Srinagar's Water Crisis Worsens due to Climate Change
cards.content: In Srinagar, a water crisis has been ongoing for years, causing daily struggles for residents like Mehak and Zamrood. The absence of a regular water supply has led to the installation of tanks and a hand pump at their homes. Climate change is affecting Doodh Ganga, a vital source of drinking water, causing erratic water supply, low flow, and dry taps. The river's water availability is decreasing due to rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and declining snowmelt. The Kashmir Valley's 24 watersheds, including Doodh Ganga, are experiencing similar impacts.

cards.title: LCD Soundsystem heads PlattForm Manchester concert series
cards.content: LCD Soundsystem has been named as the first headliner for a series of outdoor concerts at Manchester's Platt Fields Park next summer. The American rock band will perform on July 30, 2027, along with Young Fathers, Cowboy Hunters, and DJs Erol Alkan and Luka Una. The events, called PlattForm, will have a capacity of 25,000 and take place over two weekends in late July and early August. The concerts are being organized by The Warehouse Project, SJM Concerts, and Live Nation, with more artists to be announced. Platt Fields Park has previously hosted the Parklife music festival and other events, including the Flashback Festival in 2022 and 2023.

sections.title: economy
sections.description: Markets, businesses, trade and economic changes shaping the global economy.

cards.title: Report proposes cutting National Insurance to boost youth hiring
cards.content: A report by Alan Milburn proposes lowering employers' National Insurance payments and offering cash incentives to hire young workers. Many companies have complained about increased costs making it harder to take on staff. The Recruitment and Employment Confederation suggests cutting National Insurance costs could be a significant help, while the British Chambers of Commerce argues the report doesn't go far enough in addressing costs. The proposal also includes incentives for employers to hire young people who have been out of work or education, and a plan to give young people a legal right to a route into education, training, or work. Some business owners and executives believe these changes could help them hire more young workers and provide job opportunities.

cards.title: AI-Enhanced Images Raise Concerns of Misleading Homebuyers
cards.content: Estate agents are increasingly using AI to enhance property images, making homes seem more appealing. However, this practice, dubbed 'housefishing', has raised concerns among experts and homebuyers that it can mislead and waste time. Olivia Nicole, 29, was shocked to find that a five-bedroom property she viewed had been significantly altered from its online listing, with smaller rooms, different decor, and structural features changed. The AI-enhanced images, used on Rightmove, Zoopla, and Winkworth, were not clearly labeled as such, leading Olivia to feel her time was wasted. Experts warn that estate agents must use AI responsibly, labeling enhanced images and avoiding structural changes that can mislead consumers. As the trend continues to grow, concerns are rising that AI-enhanced images may become more widespread, potentially leading to more instances of 'housefishing'.

cards.title: Nscale to Build UK's Largest AI Data Centre in Loughton, Despite Microsoft Pullout
cards.content: Nscale, a tech company, has reaffirmed its plans to build the UK's largest AI data centre in Loughton, Essex, despite Microsoft's decision to pull out of the project. Microsoft had agreed to fund a supercomputer at the site, but its involvement has been terminated. Nscale is exploring alternative power sources and maintaining a strong relationship with Microsoft for other projects globally. The data centre was expected to receive its power supply by the end of this year, but this has been delayed until the 2030s due to a London-wide grid issue. The project is expected to create 250 permanent jobs when it opens.
